openers.class: Every soil map, every land-use plan and every trench on a building site depends on putting soils into named groups. That systematic grouping, by distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how soils are used, is the subject of this part. Natural systems group soils by intrinsic properties, behavior or genesis; technical systems group them by fitness for a use, from foundations to trench safety. The United States sorts its soils into six levels from order to series, Canada and Australia keep national systems of their own, and an international system edited by a working group of the International Union of Soil Sciences names soils for maps worldwide. First come the systems themselves, then the soils they name.
openers.classification-systems: An engineer, a farmer and a mapmaker can look at the same soil and file it in three different places. Engineers group soils by how they behave under foundations, a U.S. safety scheme sorts them by strength so that trenches do not collapse, and natural systems group them by their properties and genesis. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's system runs through six levels from order to series, while its predecessor had just three orders, keyed to the dominant soil-forming factors. Canada, Australia and the FAO built systems of their own, and smaller classes describe a soil's own climate, such as how wet it stays through the year.

soil-class-001.title: Putting the world's soils in order
soil-class-001.text: Long before modern science, priests in Egypt were sorting soils. Inscriptions at the temple of Horus at Edfu record a soil classification used to choose temple sites, and ancient Greek scholars devised several more. Soil classification is the systematic grouping of soils by their distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how they are used. Modern systems group soils by measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed. Soil science, engineering and environmental management all classify soils, to judge their properties and decide on suitable land use. Soil can be treated as a material, as geotechnical engineers do when judging foundations and building material, or as a resource. The major modern systems include {{ref:soil-class-006}}, the {{ref:soil-class-016}} and engineering systems that judge stability and performance, met in {{ref:soil-class-002}}. Standard systems matter because they let soils be compared across regions and uses. Knowledge of where soils occur has also grown dramatically. SoilGrids now maps soils worldwide at 1.00–0.25 km resolution, built from soil profiles and environmental data. Still, the subject keeps moving. The structure of systems, the definitions of classes and their use in the field all continue to change.

soil-class-016.title: World Reference Base: one name for a soil everywhere
soil-class-016.text: A soil can carry the same name all over the world, in English and with capital letters. That is the promise of the World Reference Base for Soil Resources, or WRB, an international system for naming soils and building soil-map legends. A working group of the {{ref:soil-hist-047}} edits it. It grew out of the {{ref:soil-class-021}} and the union's International Reference Base project. Its first edition appeared in 1998, at the world congress of soil scientists in Montpellier. That year the ISSS endorsed it as its correlation system, and it replaced the FAO scheme as the international standard. The U.S. system, {{ref:soil-class-006}}, became a correlation system too in 2014. Further editions followed in 2006, 2014, updated in 2015, and 2022; the current fourth edition is open access under a Creative Commons license. The system has just two levels. At the top sit 32 {{ref:soil-class-020}}, each refined by adding qualifiers, of which there are 202. Classes rest mainly on soil morphology, from field and laboratory data, read as an expression of how the soil formed. The climate of the soil counts only as a soil-forming factor, never as a soil characteristic. The two-level design resembles the French {{ref:soil-class-035}}, whereas the U.S. system is strongly hierarchical with six levels. The WRB is not meant to replace national systems, which may be more detailed for their own areas. The European Union uses it.

soil-class-005.title: Soil type, the word many systems avoid
soil-class-005.text: Few terms in soil science are so common, or so slippery. A soil type is a taxonomic unit: all the soils that share a defined set of properties. In hierarchical systems it usually sits at a higher or intermediate level, split into subtypes and combined into higher categories. The first U.S. classification, by Whitney in 1909, did the reverse: there the soil type was the lowest level and the mapping unit. Systems also disagree on what defines a type. German soil systematics uses mainly features made by soil formation. The WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}} add traits inherited from the parent material, and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} ignores origin. Horizons make a convenient basis, but some young soils lack clear ones, so types may rest on whole-profile properties. The WRB, for instance, defines one group by sand content alone. Many systems also define types that reflect human activity. Because the word is so general, many systems avoid it. In early U.S. mapping, 'soil type' was the original name of the soil phase, which records surface texture, slope, stoniness, saltiness and erosion.

soil-class-006.title: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series
soil-class-006.text: More than 14,000 named series are recognized in the United States, and every one sits in a single family tree. That tree is USDA soil taxonomy, the classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the {{ref:soil-hist-051}}. It sorts soils by their properties into six levels. From most general to most specific they are order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series. The country recognizes 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups and about 4,500 families. Every class rests on properties that can be measured: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content. Guy Donald Smith, who directed the USDA's investigations for mapping soils, developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural system of 1938, described in {{ref:soil-class-012}}. Work began by 1945. A series of 'approximations' followed, the 7th in 1960. The taxonomy itself appeared in 1975 with 10 orders, and a revised edition in 1999 had 12. It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide land use and the management of soil. It also supplies the core criteria for the units on U.S. maps of soils. Order names all end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed.

soil-class-021.title: The FAO map legend that became a world system
soil-class-021.text: The first truly international soil classification began life as the key to a map. The FAO soil classification, developed by the Food and Agriculture Organization, is a supra-national system that generalizes how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors. It started as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO map of the world's soils, published from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million. Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend. It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'. Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with soil phases, three texture classes and three slope classes. Simple and broad, it fitted most soils from field descriptions alone. It was meant for continental maps, not local ones. The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings, and it still underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database. United Nations projects applied the system, and many countries adapted it. Many of its names are known widely, with similar meanings. In the 1974 legend, thin soils on calcareous rock were called Rendzinas and those on acid rock were called {{ref:soil-class-040}}. The WRB replaced it in 1998.

soil-class-023.title: Canada's system, built for cool-climate soils
soil-class-023.text: Canada classifies its soils with a system closer to the U.S. one than any other, yet built to cover only Canadian soils. Introduced in 1955, it was designed to separate soils formed by soil-forming processes in cool climates. Earlier Canadian work had used U.S.-like systems. It has five levels: order, great group, subgroup, family and series. It drops the suborder, and it separates sodium-affected and waterlogged soils at the order level, as the {{ref:soil-class-029}} and the {{ref:soil-class-028}}. Ten orders sit at the top. Below them, 31 great groups reflect differences in how the soils formed. The unit classified is the pedon, a 3-dimensional body of soil commonly 1 meter across and 1 to 2 meters deep. A key sorts it using horizon thickness, Munsell color and pH. Subgroups follow the sequence of horizons and often intergrade toward other orders. Families add parent material and the climate of the soil. A series name such as Breton implies all the properties of its order, great group, subgroup and family, which supports many judgments of land suitability. Class limits are arbitrary, since nature has few sharp breaks in the soil continuum. The system changes as mapping and research add knowledge, and recent research proposes a new order for soils that are shallow or over bedrock.

soil-class-022.title: Australia's fifteen orders for an old, weathered land
soil-class-022.text: Australia's soils needed names of their own, many of them shaped by an arid, strongly weathered continent. The Australian Soil Classification is the general-purpose, hierarchical system now used to describe and classify them. It has five levels: order, suborder, great group, subgroup and family. Ray Isbell, a retired CSIRO soil scientist, developed it and first published it in 1996. Later editions came in 2002, 2010 and March 2021. It superseded the Factual Key of 1960 and the {{ref:soil-class-046}} of 1968. Since Isbell's death in 2001, the National Committee on Soil and Terrain has led its updates. Its fifteen orders run from {{ref:soil-class-044}} and Calcarosols to Sodosols, Tenosols and Vertosols. In seven orders, suborders name the dominant color of the upper B2 horizon: Red, Brown, Yellow, Grey or Black. One of those orders is {{ref:soil-found-070}}, so a soil there takes a color and an order as its name. Other orders have their own suborders. Hydrosols, for instance, split into Intertidal, Supratidal, Salic, Redoxic and other Hydrosols. The system defines soil types without asking whether their properties result from soil formation. Some names translate directly: soils called {{ref:soil-class-098}} elsewhere are Organosols here, and the {{ref:soil-class-138}} becomes the Podosol.

soil-class-002.title: How engineers classify soil to build on it
soil-class-002.text: To an engineer, soil is a material to build on or to build with. Engineering soil classification groups soils by the properties that matter when they support foundations or serve as building material. Modern systems are designed to move easily from field observations to basic predictions of how a soil will behave. In North America the most common is the Unified Soil Classification System, or USCS. It and the fuller engineering description are standardized in ASTM D 2487. Europe's ISO 14688 closely resembles the USCS but codes soils differently. It also adds an intermediate-plasticity class for silts and clays. In the United States, the {{ref:soil-class-036}} rates soils and aggregates for pavement construction. The Modified Burmister system works like the USCS but codes more properties. Moderately organic soils count as subdivisions of silts and clays. They are told apart by how their plasticity and Atterberg limits change on drying. A full geotechnical description goes further than any code. It adds color, moisture and strength in place, and more detail about the material than the USCS code carries.

soil-class-003.title: Natural classes and technical classes
soil-class-003.text: A soil can be classified for what it is, or for what it is good for. Natural systems group soils by their intrinsic properties, behavior or genesis. Technical systems group them by fitness for a particular use. Experience shows that natural classes can be interpreted for many different uses. Some natural systems, such as the French {{ref:soil-class-035}}, rest on presumed soil genesis. USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB use morphology and laboratory tests as the criteria for their hierarchical classes. Each system's approach reflects its own ideas of how soils form and of which features matter for land use. In U.S. soil mapping the two kinds meet. Map units classed by soil taxonomy are also sorted into technical classes such as Land Capability Classes, {{ref:soil-water-119}} and {{ref:soil-agri-088}}. A third route is numerical classification, or ordination. It groups soil individuals by multivariate statistics such as cluster analysis, producing natural groups without any inference about genesis.

soil-class-011.title: Moisture regimes: how wet a soil stays all year
soil-class-011.text: A desert soil may stay moist for less than 90 consecutive days; a waterlogged soil may sit saturated and almost airless. A soil moisture regime is a class describing how wet a soil stays through the year, defined by the groundwater table and the water available to plants. It often reflects climate, and it is a major control on the productivity of land ecosystems, farms included. In USDA soil taxonomy, regime names modify soil names at the suborder level. Aquic soils are saturated and almost free of oxygen long enough to show gleying and mottling; they are common in {{ref:soil-water-124}} areas. At the other end, aridic soils are dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days, as in deserts. Soils of the {{ref:soil-found-101}} stay moist enough for plants year-round in most years and are common in humid regions. Between that regime and aridic soils lies the {{ref:soil-class-041}} regime. There moisture is usually available in the growing season, but severe droughts occur; such soils are common in semi-arid regions. Xeric soils belong to Mediterranean-type climates, with cool, moist winters and long summer droughts.

soil-class-012.title: The 1938 U.S. system and its three orders
soil-class-012.text: Before modern soil taxonomy, the United States sorted soils by what had made them. The 1938 system divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors. It grew from Curtis Marbut's scheme, begun in 1920, which became the 1935 system. Modified, it was published in the 1938 Yearbook of Agriculture, Soils and Men. Its {{ref:soil-class-015}} order reflected climate and vegetation. Its {{ref:soil-class-013}} order reflected a local factor of relief or parent material strong enough to override them. At the top level, soils were split into carbonate-rich pedocals of drier climates and the {{ref:soil-class-042}} group, rich in aluminum and iron. Its root 'alfer' later became part of a modern order name, {{ref:soil-class-090}}. The 1938 scheme was a strictly natural system, and after 1938 classifying individual series under it met with mixed success. Work on a replacement began by 1945.

soil-class-004.title: OSHA soil types: keeping trench walls standing
soil-class-004.text: On a U.S. building site, three letters decide how a trench wall is held back. The OSHA soil classification is a U.S. workplace-safety scheme that sorts soils by strength, so that excavations and trenches can be protected against collapse. It uses three soil types plus stable rock. Type A soils are cohesive and plastic, with unconfined compressive strength above 1.5 tsf (144 kPa). Type B lies between 0.5 tsf (48 kPa) and 1.5 tsf. Type C falls below 0.5 tsf, or is granular or seeping. The lateral earth pressure each type induces rises from 25 psf per foot of depth for Type A to 45 for Type B and 80 for Type C. Each type dictates sloping, shoring or shielding, for safety rather than for the study of soil formation.

soil-class-017.title: The diagnostic toolkit behind every WRB name
soil-class-017.text: Every soil name in the WRB rests on a checklist of named features. These are its diagnostics: diagnostic horizons, diagnostic properties and diagnostic materials. Diagnostic horizons are typical products of soil formation with a minimum thickness, so they form a recognizable layer. Diagnostic properties are typical results of soil-forming processes, or they reflect particular conditions of soil formation. Diagnostic materials influence or indicate soil formation, and they may be inherited from the parent material or produced by soil formation. Each has a name, such as argic horizon, stagnic properties or fluvic material. Organic carbon draws one boundary. Mineral material has less than 20% organic carbon; organic material has 20% or more. Diagnostic horizons entered the international system from the 1960 '7th approximation' of USDA soil taxonomy, by way of the FAO legend. Only the diagnostic criteria decide whether a diagnostic is present in a soil.

soil-class-020.title: The 32 Reference Soil Groups, in the order of the key
soil-class-020.text: The WRB sorts the world's soils into just 32 top-level classes, and it always lists them in the same order. These are the Reference Soil Groups, each with a two-letter code, arranged as the key runs. The key opens with {{ref:soil-class-098}}, soils with thick organic layers. Then come soils under strong human influence: the long and intensively farmed {{ref:soil-class-120}} and the artefact-rich {{ref:soil-class-145}}. Next are groups that limit root growth, with permafrost, thin or stony ground, a sodium-rich clayey subsoil, shrink–swell clays or soluble salts. Eight groups are set apart by iron and aluminum chemistry, among them the {{ref:soil-class-127}} and the {{ref:soil-class-138}}. Four have organic-rich mineral topsoils, led by the {{ref:soil-class-123}}. Three more accumulate secondary silica, gypsum or carbonates. Clay-enriched subsoils mark five groups, split by clay activity and by whether exchangeable aluminum exceeds base cations. The key ends with little-differentiated soils: moderately developed, built of stratified sediments, very sandy, or with no significant development at all. Group names are plural in map legends and singular everywhere else.

soil-class-010.title: Temperature regimes, measured 50 cm down
soil-class-010.text: A soil temperature regime is a class set by mean annual and seasonal temperatures 50 cm below the surface, used to classify soils in USDA soil taxonomy. Mean annual soil temperature is normally taken as mean annual air temperature plus 2 °C. Classes run from pergelic, about −8 to −4 °C, through subgelic to frigid, about 0 to 8 °C. Mesic covers 8 to 15 °C, thermic 15 to 22 °C, and hyperthermic 22 °C or higher. Where summer and winter means differ by less than 6 °C, 'iso' is added to the name. Frigid, mesic and thermic classify soils at lower levels; the cryic regime separates some higher-level groups.

soil-class-007.title: Suborders and great groups: the second and third rungs
soil-class-007.text: Xeralfs, Durixeralfs, Abruptic Durixeralfs: each added piece of the name moves a soil one level down. Suborders, the second level of USDA soil taxonomy, split each order by properties tied to soil moisture and temperature. Moisture regime names act as modifiers at this level. Great groups, the third level, split suborders by the kind and sequence of horizons. Horizons marked by clay, iron, humus or hardpans tell them apart, as do self-mixing shrink–swell clays, temperature and large amounts of salts. In the United States, forty-seven suborders and about 185 great groups are recognized. The great group Durixeralfs, for instance, holds the subgroup Abruptic Durixeralfs, which includes the San Joaquin series.

soil-class-008.title: Typic, intergrade, extragrade: the subgroup level
soil-class-008.text: Every great group has its textbook soils, its borderline soils and its misfits. The fourth level of USDA soil taxonomy, the subgroup, names each kind. A typic subgroup carries the basic, typical concept of its great group. An intergrade subgroup has properties grading toward another great group, suborder or order, but not strongly enough to place it there. Extragrade subgroups have aberrant properties that keep them out of any other class. About 1,000 subgroups are defined in the United States.

soil-class-009.title: Soil families: grouping soils by how they behave
soil-class-009.text: 'Fine-loamy, mixed, superactive, calcareous, Typic Torrifluvents' is not a list. It is the name of one soil family. The family is the fifth level of USDA soil taxonomy: soils within a subgroup that share the physical and chemical properties governing their response to farming and engineering. Families are told apart by texture, mineralogy, pH, permeability, structure, consistency, precipitation pattern and soil temperature. Sometimes the percentages of silt, sand and coarse fragments count too. About 4,500 families are recognized in the United States, and each may contain several series. The family above belongs to the suborder Fluvents and includes the Jocity series.

soil-class-037.title: Soil series: named for a town, mapped across states
soil-class-037.text: Haugan, Montana, gave its name to a soil. A soil series is named after a town or landmark near where it was first recognized, yet a series such as Hagerstown can range across several states. The series is the lowest level of USDA soil taxonomy. It groups pedons with similar pedogenesis, soil chemistry and physical properties. Their horizons match in color, texture, structure, pH, consistency, composition and arrangement in the profile, so the soils perform alike for land use. The concept dates from 1903. Series were then meant as soils alike in origin, from the same kind of rock or sediment, but differing in texture. More than 14,000 series are recognized in the United States, the most homogeneous classes in the taxonomy; another source counts even more. A series can mean two things. As a taxonomic unit it is the conceptual core of a class. As a mapping unit it outlines similar soils on the land, and the two need not fully coincide. Map units carry the name of their dominant series. In Greenbrier County, West Virginia, unit LhE is 80% Lily series, and the rest is Dekalb, Berks and less stony soils.

soil-class-038.title: State soils, official emblems like flowers and birds
soil-class-038.text: North Carolina's state soil, the Cecil, runs from Virginia to Alabama. A state soil is one that a U.S. state has chosen as having special significance to it. Every state has selected one, and twenty have been established by law, giving them the same standing as official state flowers and birds. Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands have chosen representative soils too. California picked San Joaquin in 1997, Oklahoma named Port Silt Loam in 1987, and Illinois chose Drummer in 2001.
